title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Electio — Scripture senses (nation / office)
latin: 2. Jam veniamus ad explicationem illorum trium vocabulorum, quae subinde recurrent in tota nostra futura disputatione. Primum est Electio: Quod vocabulum in sacris Scripturis diversimode usurpatur. Nam aliquando designat separationem alicujus gentis, ad participationem communem verbi & aliorum mediorum, quibus homines ordinare perducuntur ad salutem. Sic Deus elegisse dicitur nationem Judaeorum, aliis gentibus praeteritis. Te elegit Jehovah Deus tuus, ut sis populus peculiaris prae omnibus populis, &c. Deut. vii.6. Aliquando vox haec denotat separationem certae alicujus personae ad munus aliquod sive officium vel in Republica vel in ecclesia. Sic Deus dicitur Saulum elegisse in regem Judaeorum: Videte quem elegerit Jehovah, 1 Sam. x.24. & Christus duodecim sic elegit in Apostolos: Nonne ego vos duodecim elegi, Johan. vi.70. De hisce electionibus non jam quaeritur: quamvis & in his ac caeteris ejusmodi, observare liceat electionem semper significare alicujus aut aliquorum e numero plurium separationem ad specialem finem ab agente intentum.
pass_a: 2. Now let us come to the explanation of those three vocabularies which will repeatedly recur in our whole future disputation. The first is Election: Which vocabulary is used diversely in the sacred Scriptures. For sometimes it designates the separation of some nation, unto the common participation of the word and of other means by which human beings are ordinarily led through unto salvation. So God is said to have elected the nation of the Jews, other nations having been passed by. Jehovah your God elected you, that you might be a peculiar people before all peoples, etc. Deuteronomy 7:6. Sometimes this voice denotes the separation of some certain person unto some charge or office either in the commonwealth or in the church. So God is said to have elected Saul into king of the Jews: See whom Jehovah has elected, 1 Samuel 10:24. And Christ thus elected the twelve into Apostles: Did I not elect you twelve, John 6:70. Concerning these elections it is not now inquired: although also in these and the rest of this sort it is permitted to observe that election always signifies the separation of someone or of some from the number of many unto a special end intended by the agent.
pass_b: 2. Let us now explain the three words that will keep returning through the whole dispute ahead. First is Election. Scripture uses that word in more than one way. Sometimes it means setting a people apart to share the word and the ordinary means by which people are led to salvation. So God is said to have chosen the Jewish nation and passed by the other nations. "The Lord your God has chosen you to be a people for his own possession, out of all the peoples," and so on ([[Deuteronomy 7:6 >> Bible:Deuteronomy 7:6]]). Sometimes the same word means setting a particular person apart for an office in the state or in the church. So God is said to have chosen Saul as king of the Jews: "See whom the Lord has chosen" ([[1 Samuel 10:24 >> Bible:1 Samuel 10:24]]); and Christ chose the Twelve as apostles: "Did I not choose you, the twelve?" ([[John 6:70 >> Bible:John 6:70]]). Those elections are not our question now. Still, in them and in every case of the same kind, election always means taking someone — or some — out of a larger number for a special end the agent intends.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Electio proper — glory; Thomas; vs praedestinatio
latin: Electio igitur, de qua nobis agendum erit, denotat singularem actionem voluntatis Divinae ab aeterno separantis quosdam ad finem gloriae seu vitae aeternae, aliis praeteritis. Atque haec electio, sicuti etiam & dilectio, praesupponitur praedestinationi, ut recte annotavit Thomas. Nam omnes praedestinati intelliguntur electi & dilecti: Dilecti, quatenus Deus vult illis bonum aeternae vitae; electi, quatenus vult illis hoc bonum quod non vult aliis. Proprie igitur & recte sumpta electio solum finem respicit, & est voluntas Divina conferendi gloriam singularibus quibusdam personis, cum praeteritione aliorum. Quanquam fatendum est, a Theologis nonnunquam confundi electionem cum praedestinatione: Quando vero distinguuntur, electio praecipue & proprie refertur ad ipsum finem, uti dictum est; praedestinatio ad media, uti nunc ostendetur.
pass_a: Election therefore, concerning which it will be for us to treat, denotes the singular action of the Divine will from eternity separating certain ones unto the end of glory or of eternal life, others having been passed by. And this election, just as also love, is presupposed to predestination, as Thomas rightly annotated. For all the predestined are understood as elect and beloved: Beloved, insofar as God wills to them the good of eternal life; elect, insofar as he wills to them this good which he does not will to others. Properly therefore and rightly taken, election regards the end alone, and is the Divine will of conferring glory upon certain singular persons, with the passing-by of others. Although it must be confessed that by theologians election is sometimes confused with predestination: But when they are distinguished, election is chiefly and properly referred to the end itself, as has been said; predestination to the means, as will now be shown.
pass_b: The election we must treat, then, is the singular act of the Divine will that from eternity sets certain ones apart for the end of glory — eternal life — and passes others by. Thomas rightly notes that this election, like love, is presupposed to predestination. All the predestined are understood as elect and beloved: beloved insofar as God wills them the good of eternal life; elect insofar as he wills them that good and does not will it to others. Taken properly, election looks only to the end: it is God's will to confer glory on particular persons while passing others by. Theologians do sometimes blur election with predestination. When the words are kept apart, election belongs chiefly to the end itself; predestination belongs to the means — as we will now show.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Praedestinatio — dual use; school sense
latin: Venio igitur ad vocabulum Praedestinationis, quod aliquando, licet raro, in malam etiam partem usurpatur a Theologis, nimirum pro destinatione ad mortem. Sic Augustinus Tract. 48. in Johan.: Quomodo, inquit, istis dixit, Non estis ex ovibus meis? quia videbat eos ad sempiternum interitum praedestinatos, non ad vitam aeternam sui sanguinis pretio comparatos. Et 15. De civit. cap. 1. Duo dicit esse civitates vel societates hominum; quarum una praedestinata est in aeternum regnare cum Deo, altera aeternum supplicium subire cum diabolo. Sic etiam nonnunquam loquuntur Augustini discipuli, Prosper, & Fulgentius. Quinetiam Patres in Concilio Valentino confitentur praedestinationem electorum ad vitam, & praedestinationem impiorum ad mortem. Sed nos (quod jam fere obtinuit in Schola Theologorum) praedestinationis & praedestinatorum vocabula arctamus ad illam providentiam Dei specialem, qua ab aeterno proposuit illorum salutem efficacibus mediis procurare, quos in Christo elegit: & conformiter huic aeterno proposito, eorundem salutem in tempore efficaciter & infallibiliter operatur.
pass_a: I come therefore to the vocabulary of Predestination, which sometimes, though rarely, is used by theologians even in a bad part, namely for destination unto death. So Augustine, Tractate 48 on John: How, he says, did he say to those, You are not from my sheep? because he was seeing them predestined unto everlasting destruction, not compared unto eternal life by the price of his blood. And City of God 15 chapter 1. He says there are two cities or societies of human beings; of which one is predestined to reign forever with God, the other to undergo eternal punishment with the devil. So also Augustine's disciples Prosper and Fulgentius sometimes speak. Moreover the Fathers in the Council of Valence confess the predestination of the elect unto life, and the predestination of the impious unto death. But we (which has now nearly obtained in the School of the Theologians) narrow the vocabularies of predestination and of the predestined unto that special providence of God by which from eternity he proposed to procure by efficacious means the salvation of those whom he elected in Christ: and conformably to this eternal purpose, he efficaciously and infallibly works their salvation in time.
pass_b: I turn next to Predestination. Theologians sometimes — though rarely — use that word for a bad end too: destination to death. So Augustine on John, Tractate 48: How did he say to them, "You are not of my sheep"? Because he saw them predestined to everlasting ruin, not purchased for eternal life by the price of his blood. And in City of God 15.1 he says there are two cities or societies of human beings: one predestined to reign forever with God, the other to suffer eternal punishment with the devil. Augustine's disciples Prosper and Fulgentius sometimes speak the same way. The Fathers at the Council of Valence even confess a predestination of the elect to life and a predestination of the ungodly to death. We, following what has nearly become school usage, narrow "predestination" and "the predestined" to that special providence of God by which from eternity he proposed to secure, by efficacious means, the salvation of those he chose in Christ — and, matching that eternal purpose, he works their salvation in time efficaciously and without fail.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Praedestinatio — two acts; Augustine; Aquinas arrow
latin: In praedestinatione ergo considerare possumus duos actus, unum voluntatis Divinae, alterum intellectus. Ad voluntatis actum pertinet, velle huic singulari personae salutem, eligere illum prae aliis, misereri ejus, & aliorum non misereri: quem tamen actum (ut antea observavimus) Aquinas putat esse praevium praedestinationi, & electionem appellat. Ad intellectus actum pertinet, praescire, & dirigere per media infallibilia hasce certas personas ad finem illis destinatum. Atque in hoc potissimum proprius & peculiaris praedestinationis actus versatur. Huc facit Augustiniana illa praedestinationis descriptio, Praedestinatio nihil aliud est quam praescientia & praeparatio beneficiorum Dei, quibus certissime liberantur quicunque liberantur. Nos igitur per praedestinationem semper intelligimus hanc providentiae Divinae partem quae electos suos per media infallibilia dirigit & perducit ad finem aeternae beatitudinis. Quanta sit necessitas hujus praedestinationis exinde patet, quod cum vita gloriae sit finis superans virtutem naturae humanae, non sufficit ad ejus consecutionem quod ex Dei gratuita bonitate eligamur solummodo ad hunc finem, nisi insuper per Divinam sapientiam & potentiam media apta & infallibilia nobis suppeditentur, quorum adminiculo dirigamur ad eundem. Similitudine non inepta hoc illustratur ab Aquinate. Sicut sagitta, quae primo ex proposito sagittarii destinatur ad certum scopum, mox virtute ejusdem, mediante arcu, ad eundem dirigitur & quasi transmittitur: sic quaelibet persona, quae ab aeterno ex proposito Dei destinatur ad scopum vitae aeternae, in tempore, ejusdem virtute, mediante gratia efficaci, ad hanc metam gloriae dirigitur, & tandem perducitur. Atque haec ratio transmittendi electos in vitam aeternam, quatenus ab omni aeternitate in mente Divina existere intelligitur, praedestinatio nominatur.
pass_a: In predestination therefore we can consider two acts, one of the Divine will, the other of the intellect. To the act of will it belongs to will salvation to this singular person, to elect him before others, to have mercy on him, and not to have mercy on others: which act nevertheless (as we observed before) Aquinas thinks to be previous to predestination, and calls election. To the act of intellect it belongs to foreknow, and to direct through infallible means these certain persons unto the end destined for them. And in this chiefly the proper and peculiar act of predestination is versed. That Augustinian description of predestination makes for this: Predestination is nothing other than the foreknowledge and preparation of the benefits of God, by which whoever are liberated are most certainly liberated. We therefore by predestination always understand this part of Divine providence which directs and leads through its elect by infallible means unto the end of eternal beatitude. How great the necessity of this predestination is appears from this, that since the life of glory is an end surpassing the virtue of human nature, it does not suffice for its obtainment that from God's free goodness we be elected only unto this end, unless moreover through Divine wisdom and power apt and infallible means are supplied to us, by whose aid we may be directed unto the same. By a not inept likeness this is illustrated by Aquinas. Just as an arrow, which first from the purpose of the archer is destined unto a certain mark, presently by his virtue, the bow mediating, is directed unto the same and as it were transmitted: so any person who from eternity from God's purpose is destined unto the mark of eternal life, in time, by the same one's virtue, efficacious grace mediating, is directed unto this goal of glory, and at last is led through. And this account of transmitting the elect into eternal life, insofar as it is understood to exist from all eternity in the Divine mind, is named predestination.
pass_b: In predestination, then, we can mark two acts: one of the Divine will, one of the intellect. The will's act is to will salvation for this particular person, to choose him before others, to show him mercy and not show mercy to others — an act Aquinas (as we noted earlier) treats as prior to predestination and calls election. The intellect's act is to foreknow, and to direct these particular persons by infallible means to the end destined for them. That second act is where predestination proper chiefly lives. Augustine's description fits here: Predestination is nothing other than God's foreknowledge and preparation of the benefits by which whoever are set free are set free with certainty. So by predestination we always mean that part of Divine providence which directs its elect by infallible means and leads them through to eternal blessedness. How necessary this is becomes clear once you see that the life of glory surpasses what human nature can reach: free election to that end is not enough unless Divine wisdom and power also supply fit, infallible means that guide us there. Aquinas's likeness is not strained. An arrow is first aimed at a mark by the archer's purpose; then by his power, through the bow, it is sent toward that same mark. So every person destined from eternity by God's purpose for the mark of eternal life is, in time, by that same power, through efficacious grace, directed to glory's goal and at last brought there. That whole account of transmitting the elect into eternal life — as it is understood to stand from all eternity in the Divine mind — is what we call predestination.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Reprobatio — Scripture voice vs school sense
latin: De opposito Reprobationis vocabulo jam paucis dicemus. Ad vocem quod attinet, in sacris Scripturis reprobus & reprobare referuntur potius ad praesentem hominum impiorum conditionem, quam ad aeternam Dei de illis ordinationem. Nam ἀδόκιμος sive reprobus appellatur qui impie vivit, nec gerit se pro filio Dei, sed factis ostendit se esse rejectitium, spurium & adulterinum: Atque Deus tales repellere, rejicere sive reprobare dicitur propter illorum impuritatem, sicut aurifices rejiciunt nummos adulterinos. Quinetiam apud Augustinum (qui hanc materiam uberius & dilucidius quam caeteri Patres tractavit) reproborum & reprobandi vocabula, eo sensu quo nunc in Schola Theologorum frequentantur, aut raro, aut non omnino occurrunt. Sed tamen sciendum est rem ipsam in sacris Scripturis aperte contineri. Primo, quando ea affirmantur in sacris Scripturis unde clara & necessaria consecutione deducitur quorundam reprobatio: Ut cum certae quaedam & signatae personae dicuntur electi & praedestinati a Deo ante jacta mundi fundamenta. Electio enim aliquorum praeteritionem sive rejectionem aliorum infert. Secundo, quando verbis aequivalentibus reprobationis decretum exprimitur: ut cum Deus dicitur quosdam nunquam nosse, non dedisse Christo, nolle quorundam misereri, non scripsisse quorundam nomina in libro vitae, & id genus alia, quae liquido probant, apud Divinam mentem & voluntatem fuisse discrimen electorum & non-electorum ab aeterno. Postremo, licet Augustinus, aliique Patres non multum utantur hoc vocabulo reprobationis, tamen aliis utuntur quae perinde valent. Nam quos Schola appellat reprobatos, illi vocant praescitos & praedestinatos ad interitum.
pass_a: Concerning the opposite vocabulary of Reprobation we will now say a few things. As to the voice, in the sacred Scriptures reprobus and reprobare are referred rather to the present condition of impious human beings than to the eternal ordination of God concerning them. For ἀδόκιμος or reprobate is called one who lives impiously, and does not bear himself as a son of God, but by deeds shows himself to be rejectitious, spurious, and adulterine: And God is said to repel, reject, or reprobate such ones because of their impurity, just as goldsmiths reject adulterine coins. Moreover in Augustine (who treated this matter more richly and more clearly than the other Fathers) the vocabularies of the reprobate and of reprobating, in that sense in which they are now frequented in the School of the Theologians, occur either rarely or not at all. But nevertheless it must be known that the thing itself is openly contained in the sacred Scriptures. First, when those things are affirmed in the sacred Scriptures whence by clear and necessary consequence the reprobation of certain ones is deduced: As when certain marked persons are said to be elect and predestined by God before the foundations of the world were laid. For the election of some imports the passing-by or rejection of others. Second, when by equivalent words the decree of reprobation is expressed: as when God is said never to have known certain ones, not to have given them to Christ, to be unwilling to have mercy on certain ones, not to have written certain ones' names in the book of life, and other things of that kind, which liquidly prove that there was in the Divine mind and will a discrimination of elect and non-elect from eternity. Finally, although Augustine and the other Fathers do not much use this vocabulary of reprobation, nevertheless they use others which are equally valid. For those whom the School calls reprobates, they call foreknown and predestined unto destruction.
pass_b: On the opposite word, Reprobation, a few points. As for the bare term, Scripture's "reprobate" and "to reprobate" point more to the present state of the ungodly than to God's eternal decree about them. ἀδόκιμος — a reprobate — is one who lives ungodly, does not carry himself as a son of God, and by his deeds shows himself counterfeit, spurious, adulterate. God is said to reject or reprobate such people because of that impurity, as goldsmiths throw out counterfeit coins. Even in Augustine — who treated this matter more richly and clearly than the other Fathers — "reprobate" and "reprobating" in the school sense barely appear, or do not appear at all. Still, the thing itself is plainly in Scripture. First, when Scripture affirms what forces the reprobation of some by clear necessary consequence: as when certain named persons are said elect and predestined by God before the world's foundations were laid. Election of some imports passing by — rejecting — others. Second, when equivalent phrases express the decree: God is said never to have known some, not to have given them to Christ, to refuse mercy to some, not to have written some names in the book of life — and the like, which plainly prove that from eternity the Divine mind and will marked a difference between elect and non-elect. Finally, though Augustine and the other Fathers seldom use the school word "reprobation," they use other words that mean the same. Those the School calls reprobates, they call foreknown and predestined to destruction.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Reprobatio — opposite act; Bannes; negative vs positive
latin: Sed misso vocabulo, veniamus ad rem. Sicuti igitur eligere & praedestinare denotat illum aeternum actum Divinae voluntatis, quo decrevit quasdam personas dirigere ad beatitudinem infallibiliter consequendam; sic reprobare denotat oppositum actum Divinae voluntatis, quo decrevit permittere quasdam personas ab hoc fine beatitudinis deficere & excidere. Atque hoc vel maxime convenit providentiae Divinae, ut permittat aliquem defectum in rebus quae providentiae ejus subduntur. Videte Aquinatem, part. 1. qu. 23. art. 6. In hac reprobatione duos quasi actus Divinae voluntatis consideramus. Prior est, nolle eligere ad beatitudinem infallibiliter consequendam. Atque cur hic actus potius ad Judam quam ad Petrum terminetur, nulla datur ratio ex parte reprobati, sed referendum est ad libertatem Divinae voluntatis. Sic Bannes: In singulari, quare Deus hos elegerit, illos reprobaverit, non habet causam adaequatam, nisi Divinam voluntatem. Et eodem in articulo dicit, hanc praedestinationem aliquorum, & reprobationem aliorum esse manifestationem maximae libertatis, quam habet Divina voluntas circa dispensationem bonorum supernaturalium: quae libertas est magna perfectio Divina. Hunc actum, quem nos appellamus praeteritionem sive non-electionem, Bellarminus vocat actum negativum reprobationis. Sed illud hic cavendum est, ne cum Scoto putemus Dei voluntatem respectu reproborum, quos non eligit, sed praeterit, habere se mere negative. Nam in hoc actu, quem per negationem significamus, continetur expressa & affirmata voluntas Dei, non innuitur negata aut suspensa actio volendi circa reproborum deficientiam a beatitudine. Affirmative ergo explicari debet & intelligi hic actus Divinae voluntatis, & non solum negative. Nam praeteritio sive non-electio involvit hosce actus affirmativos: volo permittere Judam deficere a vita aeterna: volo & decerno Judae non dare eam gratiam specialem, quam si reciperet, perveniret ad vitam aeternam. Haec de priori actu reprobationis. Posterior est, destinare ad poenam. Atque hic actus terminatur ad reprobatum, sicuti praecognitus & praevisus est peccato contaminatus, idque ex vitio propriae voluntatis. Hanc Scotus vocat privativam reprobationem; Bellarminus, actum positivum reprobationis. Et designat voluntatem damnandi personam reprobatam. Porro, notandum est, erga ipsos reprobatos exhiberi a Deo quaedam effecta quae non fluunt a reprobatione illorum; ut quod creentur, quod vocentur ad cognitionem Evangelii, quod illustrentur cognitione supernaturali: nam haec, & alia ejusmodi, effecta sunt communis amoris, & communis providentiae Divinae, non reprobationis.
pass_a: But the vocabulary having been dismissed, let us come to the thing. Just as therefore to elect and to predestinate denotes that eternal act of the Divine will by which he decreed to direct certain persons unto beatitude to be infallibly obtained; so to reprobate denotes the opposite act of the Divine will by which he decreed to permit certain persons to fail and fall away from this end of beatitude. And this most greatly agrees with Divine providence, that it should permit some defect in things which are subjected to its providence. See Aquinas, part 1 question 23 article 6. In this reprobation we consider two quasi-acts of the Divine will. The prior is, to be unwilling to elect unto beatitude to be infallibly obtained. And why this act is terminated rather to Judas than to Peter, no reason is given from the side of the reprobate, but it must be referred to the liberty of the Divine will. So Báñez: In the singular, why God elected these, reprobated those, has no adequate cause except the Divine will. And in the same article he says that this predestination of some and reprobation of others is a manifestation of the greatest liberty which the Divine will has concerning the dispensation of supernatural goods: which liberty is a great Divine perfection. This act, which we call passing-by or non-election, Bellarmine calls the negative act of reprobation. But this must here be guarded against, lest with Scotus we think the will of God with respect to the reprobate, whom he does not elect but passes by, holds itself merely negatively. For in this act, which we signify through negation, there is contained an expressed and affirmed will of God; there is not implied a denied or suspended action of willing concerning the reprobates' falling short from beatitude. Affirmatively therefore this act of the Divine will ought to be explained and understood, and not only negatively. For passing-by or non-election involves these affirmative acts: I will to permit Judas to fail from eternal life; I will and decree not to give to Judas that special grace which, if he received it, he would arrive at eternal life. These concerning the prior act of reprobation. The posterior is, to destine unto punishment. And this act is terminated to the reprobate as he is precognized and foreseen contaminated by sin, and that from the fault of his own will. This Scotus calls privative reprobation; Bellarmine, the positive act of reprobation. And it designates the will of damning the reprobate person. Further, it must be noted that toward the reprobates themselves certain effects are exhibited by God which do not flow from their reprobation; as that they are created, that they are called to the knowledge of the Gospel, that they are illuminated with supernatural knowledge: for these, and others of this sort, are effects of common love and of common Divine providence, not of reprobation.
pass_b: Drop the bare word; come to the thing. As to elect and to predestinate name that eternal act of the Divine will by which God decreed to direct certain persons to blessedness they will infallibly reach, so to reprobate names the opposite act: the decree to permit certain persons to fail and fall short of that end. That fits providence itself — which allows some defect in the things under its care. See Aquinas, ST I q.23 a.6. In reprobation we mark two quasi-acts of the Divine will. The first is unwillingness to elect someone to blessedness obtained without fail. Why that act lands on Judas rather than Peter has no reason on the reprobate's side; it is referred to the liberty of the Divine will. So Báñez: in the particular case, why God chose these and reprobated those has no adequate cause but the Divine will. In the same article he says this predestination of some and reprobation of others manifests the greatest liberty the Divine will has in dispensing supernatural goods — and that liberty is a great Divine perfection. The act we call passing-by or non-election, Bellarmine calls the negative act of reprobation. Guard this point: do not follow Scotus in treating God's will toward the reprobate — whom he does not choose but passes by — as merely negative. In the act we name by a negation there is an expressed, affirmative will of God; it does not mean God simply suspends willing about their falling short of blessedness. Read that act affirmatively, not only negatively. Passing-by / non-election involves affirmative decrees: I will to permit Judas to fall short of eternal life; I will and decree not to give Judas that special grace which, if he received it, would bring him to eternal life. So much for the first act. The second is to destine to punishment. That act terminates on the reprobate as foreknown and foreseen stained by sin — and that from the fault of his own will. Scotus calls this privative reprobation; Bellarmine, the positive act of reprobation. It designates the will to damn the reprobate person. Note also: God shows the reprobate certain effects that do not flow from their reprobation — that they are created, called to know the Gospel, illuminated with supernatural knowledge. Those are effects of common love and common providence, not of reprobation.

title: Cap. 1 vocabulary: Reprobatio effects; against Pelagian calumny (Prosper)
latin: Propria autem & vera effecta reprobationis negativae haec sunt: Nolle decernere efficacem liberationem personae in statu damnationis jacentis; Velle negare tali personae auxilia efficacia quibus de facto converteretur. Ultimus effectus est aeterna punitio obstinati peccatoris: qui non proprie oritur ex mera praeteritione vel non-electione, sed ex illo altero reprobationis actu, quem praedamnationem licet appellare; atque peccati praevisionem supponit, & derelictionem in eodem. Jam & illud perpendendum, effecta reprobationis non habere illam connexionem inter se, quam habent effecta praedestinationis. Nam in praedestinatione prior effectus solet esse causa posterioris; ut vocatio efficax parit fidem, fides justificationem, &c.; sed in reprobatione effectus non sunt hoc modo invicem ordinati, quamvis omnes junctim sumpti ordinentur ad unum & eundem finem, relucentiam scilicet justitiae Divinae. Ultimo, & illud contra quorumdam malevolas calumniationes animadvertendum est: Licet peccata, qualia sunt infidelitas, improbitas, obduratio, & poena hisce debita, hoc est, aeterna damnatio, in homine lapso aeque infallibiliter consequantur reprobationem, atque fides, sanctitas, perseverantia consequuntur praedestinationem, tamen non eodem modo consequuntur. Nam Deus agens ex decreto praedestinationis operatur haec priora per influxum gratiae efficacis: at ex decreto reprobationis nihil agit quo deterior efficiatur reprobatus, nihil quo vel impediatur a credendo & sancte vivendo, vel impellatur ad infidelitatem aut improbitatem. Hoc diligenter observandum est, quia tam veteres Pelagiani, quam novi, cum videant, posita reprobatione tali qualem descripsimus, neminem reproborum aut credere perseveranter, aut sancte vivere, illico clamant, nos facere Deum autorem peccati, & causam cur vel non credant, vel resilant a fide & sanctitate; Sed cum Propheta respondemus cuivis reprobo, perditio tua ex te, licet auxilium ex solo Deo. Nam reprobatio nil subtrahit de potentia ipsius reprobati, quamvis Deus erga illum non exserat illam potentiam efficacem, quam posset si vellet. Sic olim Prosper, Deus neminem boni possibilitate desoliat. Non est ergo consequens, sicut putant qui talia objiciunt, ut Deus quibus poenitentiam non dederit, resipiscentiam abstulerit; & quos non levaverit, alliserit, &c. haec ille. Longe aliter igitur se habet reprobatio in causando, quam praedestinatio. Deus praedestinans operatur omnia bona in praedestinatis per influxum gratiae, & causa efficiens proprie nominatur: sed Deus reprobans nulla operatur mala in reprobis per subtractionem gratiae, sed mala consequenter erumpunt ex corruptione naturae, quorum Deus non magis causa est, quam sol tenebrarum, quando non illuminat aerem. Haec de electione, Praedestinatione & reprobatione praefanda putavi.
pass_a: But the proper and true effects of negative reprobation are these: To be unwilling to decree the efficacious liberation of a person lying in the state of damnation; To will to deny to such a person the efficacious helps by which he would in fact be converted. The last effect is the eternal punishment of the obstinate sinner: which does not properly arise from mere passing-by or non-election, but from that other act of reprobation which it is permitted to call pre-damnation; and it presupposes the foreseeing of sin, and dereliction in the same. Now that also must be weighed, that the effects of reprobation do not have that connection among themselves which the effects of predestination have. For in predestination the prior effect is accustomed to be the cause of the posterior; as efficacious calling begets faith, faith justification, etc.; but in reprobation the effects are not ordered to one another in this mode, although all taken jointly are ordered unto one and the same end, namely the shining-forth of Divine justice. Finally, this also must be noticed against the malevolent calumnies of certain ones: Although sins such as unbelief, wickedness, hardening, and the penalty owed to these, that is, eternal damnation, follow reprobation in the fallen human being equally infallibly as faith, holiness, perseverance follow predestination, nevertheless they do not follow in the same mode. For God acting from the decree of predestination works these prior things through the influx of efficacious grace: but from the decree of reprobation he does nothing by which the reprobate is made worse, nothing by which he is either impeded from believing and living holily, or impelled unto unbelief or wickedness. This must carefully be observed, because both the old Pelagians and the new, when they see that, such reprobation as we have described having been posited, none of the reprobate either believe perseveringly or live holily, immediately cry out that we make God the author of sin, and the cause why they either do not believe or spring back from faith and holiness; But with the Prophet we answer to any reprobate, your destruction is from you, although help is from God alone. For reprobation subtracts nothing from the power of the reprobate himself, although God toward him does not put forth that efficacious power which he could if he willed. So formerly Prosper: God despoils no one of the possibility of the good. It is not therefore a consequence, as those think who object such things, that God from those to whom he has not given penitence has taken away repentance; and those whom he has not lifted, he has struck down, etc. — these are his words. Far otherwise therefore does reprobation hold itself in causing than predestination. God predestinating works all goods in the predestined through the influx of grace, and is properly named an efficient cause: but God reprobating works no evils in the reprobate through subtraction of grace, but evils consequently break forth from the corruption of nature, of which God is no more the cause than the sun is of darknesses, when it does not illuminate the air. These things concerning election, Predestination, and reprobation I have thought should be set forth beforehand.
pass_b: The proper effects of negative reprobation are these: unwillingness to decree the efficacious liberation of a person lying under damnation; and the will to deny that person the efficacious helps by which he would in fact be converted. The last effect is the eternal punishment of the obstinate sinner. That does not properly rise from mere passing-by or non-election, but from the other reprobation-act one may call pre-damnation — which presupposes foresight of sin and leaving the person in it. Weigh this too: reprobation's effects are not chained to one another the way predestination's are. In predestination the earlier effect usually causes the later — efficacious calling begets faith, faith justification, and so on. In reprobation the effects are not ordered that way, though taken together they serve one end: the shining of Divine justice. Finally, against certain malevolent slanders, mark this: In the fallen human being, sins such as unbelief, wickedness, and hardening — and the penalty due them, eternal damnation — follow reprobation as infallibly as faith, holiness, and perseverance follow predestination; yet they do not follow in the same way. Acting from the decree of predestination, God works those earlier goods by the influx of efficacious grace. From the decree of reprobation he does nothing that makes the reprobate worse, nothing that blocks believing and holy living, nothing that drives him into unbelief or wickedness. Watch that carefully. Old Pelagians and new alike see that, given reprobation as we have described it, none of the reprobate perseveres in faith or holy life — and they cry at once that we make God the author of sin and the cause why people do not believe or spring back from faith and holiness. With the Prophet we answer every reprobate: your destruction is from you, though help is from God alone. Reprobation takes nothing from the reprobate's own power; God simply does not put forth toward him the efficacious power he could put forth if he willed. So Prosper long ago: God despoils no one of the possibility of the good. It does not follow — as the objectors think — that those to whom God has not given penitence he has robbed of repentance, or that those he has not lifted he has struck down, and so on. Reprobation causes in a far different way from predestination. God predestinating works every good in the predestined by grace's influx, and is properly called an efficient cause. God reprobating works no evils in the reprobate by subtracting grace; the evils break out from nature's corruption — and God is no more their cause than the sun is cause of darkness when it does not light the air. So much I thought should be set down first on election, Predestination, and reprobation.
